standard.title: Language to appreciate and prefer
standard.description: explore how language can be used for appreciating texts and providing reasons for preferences
standard.prior_knowledge: Students explore language used to give reasons for likes, dislikes and preferences (AC9E1LA02). They have not yet used more precise vocabulary to appreciate specific textual features, or explored verbs that express degree of preference.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students can explore how language is used to appreciate texts and give reasoned explanations for preferences using more precise vocabulary.

nodes.label: Moving beyond 'I liked it'
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify that appreciation language names what specifically they are responding to, not just that they liked something.
nodes.minimum_width: Distinguish between a vague preference statement ('I liked it') and a statement that names a specific textual feature ('I liked how the author described the setting').
nodes.typical_width: Identify and practise appreciation language that names specific textual features — setting, character, language choice, illustration — across several texts.
wider: Compare appreciation statements made by different students about the same text and identify which features each person noticed
Examine book reviews or blurbs as examples of appreciation language used for an audience

response_modes.reason: Students commonly conflate 'liking' with 'appreciating'. The misconception is that preference is just emotional — widening to name what specifically is being liked (setting, character, language) resolves this. More textual examples across different features, not more repetition of the same example, is the productive move.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Rich opportunity to build a repertoire of appreciation sentence frames across different textual features. Each new feature (setting, character, word choice, illustration) adds a genuine new direction for appreciation language.
success_criteria: Student produces an appreciation statement that names a specific textual feature, not just a general response.
Student can explain what makes their statement an appreciation rather than just a preference.

nodes.label: Preference verbs and degree
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can select verbs that express different degrees of preference — liked, preferred, enjoyed, loved — and explain the difference.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify that 'liked', 'preferred' and 'enjoyed' express different degrees of preference and use at least two in a statement.
nodes.typical_width: Explore a range of preference verbs and their degrees, choose appropriate verbs for different responses, and discuss why degree matters when giving a reason.
wider: Compare how degree of preference changes the persuasiveness of a recommendation — stronger verbs create stronger recommendations
Identify preference verbs in texts by different authors and consider why they chose that degree

response_modes.reason: Distinguishing degrees of preference is a precise vocabulary task. Students need practice — trying verbs in context, comparing them, choosing between them — rather than broader contexts. Fluency in selecting the right degree verb is the target.

success_criteria: Student can use at least two different preference verbs and explain what difference in degree each conveys.
Student can select the most appropriate preference verb for a given strength of response.

nodes.label: Specific vocabulary for place and setting
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can use specific vocabulary — including place names and descriptive nouns — to make appreciation of setting more precise.
nodes.minimum_width: Replace a vague setting description ('the place') with a more specific term ('the forest', 'the outback') when appreciating a text.
nodes.typical_width: Explore how specific vocabulary for setting, including First Nations Australian language words specific to Country/Place where relevant, makes appreciation of a text more precise and vivid.
wider: Identify First Nations Australian language words specific to Country/Place used in texts and explore how using those words makes appreciation of the setting more specific and respectful
Compare appreciation of setting using general vs specific vocabulary and discuss the effect on the reader
nodes.width_opportunity_reason: First Nations Australian language words specific to Country/Place are a genuinely enriching direction here — they demonstrate that specific vocabulary is not just about adjectives but about cultural precision, adding real pedagogical richness beyond what the descriptor strictly requires.
success_criteria: Student uses a specific vocabulary term (not a vague placeholder) when appreciating the setting of a text.
Student can explain why the specific word makes their appreciation more precise.
